content: "In the 19th century, the notion that 'great men' - extraordinary individuals with exceptional talents and personalities - shape history through their sheer force of genius prevailed. This belief persisted despite the emergence of egalitarian and Marxist social theories, as well as EP Thompson's 'history from below' approach in the 1960s. Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle considered figures like Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad as heroic figures who profoundly impacted the world around them. According to Carlyle, the masses could only watch in admiration and follow the lead of these top-down influencers. Despite its absurdity, this idea has endured over time. Some individuals, mainly men, still see themselves as heroic figures with a special mission or calling to lead and save people and nations. These individuals often exhibit ruthless and arrogant behavior, believing they have unique insights and the authority to impose their views on others. However, in modern times, these so-called 'great' men are often not heroes but rather anti-heroes or villains, who wield significant power and influence. The misguided belief in the supremacy of such individuals persists, despite the fact that they may not be acting in the best interests of society as a whole."
